feedback: A comparison such as age >= 18 is an expression in its own right, and its value is a boolean: true or false. It can be stored, printed or combined like any other value, not just placed inside an if. adult does not hold the age that was tested, only the verdict. Java does not use 1 and 0 for true and false, and "true" in quotes would be a String, which is a different type.

question: x is an int. Match each rule, written in English, to the Java condition that implements it.

pairs.term: x is between 1 and 10, including both ends
x is outside the range 1 to 10

feedback: "Between" needs both tests to hold, so it is && (AND). "Outside" is satisfied by either side, so it is || (OR). "Neither 1 nor 10" means not 1 AND not 10: writing x != 1 || x != 10 would be true for every number, because no number equals both. Including the ends means >= and <=; strictly between means > and <.

correct: It does not compile: 0 < x is a boolean, and a boolean cannot be compared with 10
incorrect: It prints in range, because Java reads this as 0 < x and x < 10
It prints in range for any x, because 0 < x becomes 0 or 1, and both are below 10
It compiles, but throws an exception when the comparison is evaluated
feedback: Java evaluates 0 < x first and gets a boolean. The next step would be true < 10, and < does not accept a boolean, so the compiler rejects the line ("bad operand types"). The maths notation has to be written as two tests joined with AND: 0 < x && x < 10. (In C the chained form compiles and is quietly wrong; Java refuses it.)

question: Three boolean variables, two mixed conditions. What are the two lines of output?
feedback: Precedence among the logical operators is ! first, then &&, then ||. Line one: !a is false, b && c is false, and false || false is false. Line two: b && !c is grouped first (false), then a || false is true. Reading line two strictly left to right, as (a || b) && !c, gives false, which is the usual slip. When in doubt, add parentheses.

question: Java evaluates && and || from left to right and stops as soon as the answer is certain. With &&, the right-hand side is skipped when the left-hand side is {{1}}. With ||, the right-hand side is skipped when the left-hand side is {{2}}.
feedback: This is short-circuit evaluation. false && anything is false whatever the right side is, so Java does not look at it. true || anything is true, so again the right side is skipped. The skipped side is not evaluated at all, so any method call or division written there simply does not happen.

question: The second half of this condition would divide by zero. What does the program print?
feedback: n != 0 is false, so && short-circuits: 10 / n is never evaluated and no ArithmeticException occurs. The whole condition is false and the else branch prints safe. Swap the two halves (10 / n > 1 && n != 0) and the division runs first and crashes. Put the guard on the left.

question:
boolean done = false;

Which of these conditions evaluate to true at this point?
feedback: !done flips false to true, and the two comparisons say the same thing the long way round; !done is the idiomatic form. done = false has a single =, so it is an assignment: it compiles, stores false again, and the value of the whole expression is false, so a loop written while (done = false) never runs. not is Python; in Java it does not compile.

question: A score of 85 is supposed to earn "good". What does this chain actually print?
feedback: An if / else if chain is checked from the top, and the first true condition wins: its branch runs and the rest of the chain is skipped without being tested. 85 >= 60 is true, so pass is printed and "good" is never reached. The fix is to test the most demanding condition first: >= 90, then >= 80, then >= 60.

feedback_template: There is no else here, so these are four separate if statements, and every one of them is tested. Each condition that {{s}} satisfies adds a star, giving {{expected}}. In an else-if chain only the first true branch would run, and stars could never pass 1.

feedback: Without braces an if controls exactly one statement: the next one. Java ignores indentation completely, so the second println is not part of the if, however it is lined up, and it runs every time. hp > 0 is false, so alive is skipped and fight is printed. This is why the habit of always writing the braces is worth having.

question: Java ignores indentation, and none of these ifs has braces. Work out which if the else belongs to, then give the output.
feedback: An else always pairs with the nearest if before it that does not yet have one. Here that is if (y > 10), whatever the indentation suggests. So the inner if-else is, as a whole, the single statement controlled by if (x > 10). Since 5 > 10 is false, all of it is skipped and only C is printed. Anyone who pairs the else with the outer if expects B and then C. Braces remove the doubt.

question: The ?: operator picks one of two values. What does this print?
feedback: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse is an expression: it produces a value. a > b is false, so max takes the value after the colon, 12. Then 12 % 2 == 0 is true, so kind takes the value before the colon, "even". The ternary is a compact if-else for choosing between two values; it is not a replacement for if-else blocks that do several things.

question: The int variables a, b and big already exist. Using the conditional operator ( ? : ), write one statement that stores the larger of a and b in big.
feedback: The shape is condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse, and the whole expression is what gets assigned: big = a > b ? a : b; Any comparison that picks the larger one is accepted. The common slip is putting the two values the wrong way round, which silently stores the smaller one.

question: NPC: One value, many doors
intro: Nia stands where the corridor splits into a row of doors, each with a number chalked on it. “When ONE value decides which of many doors you take, Java has a tool made for the job.”

beats.say: A long if / else if chain would work here, but switch says it more plainly. This is the modern arrow form:
Java takes the value of coins, finds the case that matches it, and runs only what follows that arrow. default is the door for “none of the above”.

check.why: Only the matching arrow runs. With arrows, Java never carries on into the next case.

beats.say: A switch can also BE a value. This is a switch expression: each arrow hands back a value, and the whole switch is stored in a variable.
case 2, 3 means “2 or 3”. And see the semicolon after the closing brace? The whole thing is one assignment statement.

check.prompt: If coins were 3, what would food hold?
check.why: 3 is listed in case 2, 3, so that arrow supplies the value.

steps.say: A switch expression must always produce a value, so Java will not compile it unless every possible value has a door. For an int, that means you need default.

beats.say: A switch expression must always produce a value, so Java will not compile it unless every possible value has a door. For an int, that means you need default.
In older code you will meet the colon form. Read it; do not copy it.

With colons, Java does not stop at the end of a case. It keeps running down into the next case (this is called fall-through) until it meets break. Forget one break and two cases run. Arrows have no fall-through, which is why we prefer them.

outro: “The next monster hides a value behind a switch expression. Find the matching case, take what is after the arrow, ignore every other door.”

question: A switch expression chooses the value stored in kind. What is printed?
feedback: day is 6, which matches case 6, so the switch expression produces "market" and that is what kind holds. With the arrow form only the matching case is used; nothing falls through to default. case 1, 7 shows how one case can list several values.

question: This is the older colon form, and some of the break statements are missing. What is printed?
feedback: In the colon form, case labels are only entry points. Java jumps to case 2, prints B, and then falls through into case 3 because nothing stopped it, printing C. The break after C finally leaves the switch, so D is not printed. A is skipped because execution entered below it. Fall-through is the classic bug of colon-form switches; arrow-form cases cannot do this.

Each case uses the arrow -> to give its value, and default catches every value that no case names. Here default is not optional: a switch expression has to produce a value for every possible int, and without default the compiler reports that the switch "does not cover all possible input values".

question:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { body }

Put the first five things that happen when this loop runs into order, earliest first.
items: i < 3 is tested while i is 0
The body runs while i is 0
i < 3 is tested while i is 1
feedback: The initialization runs once. After that the loop cycles: test the condition, run the body, run the update, and back to the test. The condition is tested before the very first pass, so a for loop can run zero times, and the update happens after the body, never before it.

question: NPC: Counting the passes of a loop
intro: Nia holds up one hand, fingers folded. “Most loop bugs are the same bug: the loop runs one time too many, or one too few. So we count. On fingers, if we must.”

beats.say: How many times does this bell ring?
Do not guess. List the values i takes while the condition i <= 6 is true: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

check.prompt: How many values are in that list?
check.why: Count them: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 is five values, so the body runs five times.

steps.say: The trap is to subtract: 6 - 2 is 4. But both ends are included, the 2 and the 6. So with <= the number of passes is end - start + 1.

beats.say: The trap is to subtract: 6 - 2 is 4. But both ends are included, the 2 and the 6. So with <= the number of passes is end - start + 1.

steps.say:
Now change <= to < and the last value is lost: i takes 2, 3, 4, 5. With < the number of passes is simply end - start.
Being wrong by exactly one like this has a name: an off-by-one error. The cure is always the same. Write out the first value and the last value that really get used.

beats.say: Now change <= to < and the last value is lost: i takes 2, 3, 4, 5. With < the number of passes is simply end - start.
Being wrong by exactly one like this has a name: an off-by-one error. The cure is always the same. Write out the first value and the last value that really get used.

check.prompt: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)  How many passes?
check.why: i takes 0 through 9. With <, the count is end - start: 10 - 0 = 10.

outro: “A monster ahead will hand you a loop with numbers of its own. First value, last value, then count.”

feedback_template: i takes every value from {{a}} up to and including {{b}}, because the condition is <=. Both ends count, so the number of passes is {{b}} - {{a}} + 1 = {{expected}}. Subtracting without the + 1 is the classic off-by-one error.

Trace count: it starts at {{start}} and grows by {{step}} each pass, and the loop goes on while count is still below {{limit}}. The condition is tested before every pass, so the loop ends at the first value that is {{limit}} or more, after {{expected}} passes. count does not have to land exactly on the limit; it only has to stop being less than it.

question: This loop updates with ++i instead of the usual i++. What is printed?
feedback: The update part of a for loop runs after the body on every pass, whichever way it is written. ++i and i++ both add 1 to i, and nothing here uses the value of the update expression itself, so the loop behaves exactly like the i++ version: the first pass still sees i as 0. Expecting 123 comes from thinking ++i happens before the first pass.

question: A block should repeat while count is less than 10, and the block itself increases count. Which header does that?
feedback: The condition goes in parentheses and the block follows directly. The version with a semicolon compiles, which is what makes it dangerous: the ; is an empty statement and becomes the entire loop body, so count never changes and the program hangs forever without reaching the block. =< is not an operator (it is <=, and that would run one extra pass). Leaving out the parentheses is legal in Python and Swift but not in Java.

question: Both loops use the same condition, and n starts at 10. What is printed?
feedback: A while loop tests its condition before each pass, so with 10 < 5 false from the start its body runs zero times and no W appears. A do-while runs its body first and tests afterwards, so its body always runs at least once: D is printed, n becomes 11, and only then is 11 < 5 found false. Use do-while when the first pass must happen whatever the data, such as asking for input before checking it.

question: Inside a loop body, what does the statement continue; do?
correct: It skips the rest of this pass and moves on to the next pass of the loop
incorrect: It leaves the loop at once and carries on with the code after the loop
It does nothing on its own: it marks where the loop resumes after a pause
It restarts the whole loop from the beginning, with the counter reset too
feedback: continue abandons the current pass only. In a for loop the update (such as i++) still runs, the condition is tested again, and the loop carries on if it is true. Leaving the loop altogether is a different statement. Nothing in Java resets a loop counter for you.

question: The Java keyword that ends a loop immediately, abandoning any passes that were still to come, is ___.
feedback: break jumps straight out of the nearest enclosing loop, and execution carries on with the first statement after it. It is the same keyword that ends a case in a colon-form switch. Compare continue, which gives up only the current pass and keeps looping.

break ends the whole loop, so everything from that pass onward is lost: breaking at 3 leaves 12, and breaking on the very first pass (1 < 3) leaves nothing. continue skips only the print of the current pass: skipping 3 alone gives 1245, skipping everything above 3 gives 123, and skipping everything below 3 gives 345.

feedback_template: The break is tested before sum += i on each pass, so when i reaches {{k}} the loop ends without adding {{k}}. Only the values below {{k}} were added, giving {{expected}}. The header says i <= 10, but break overrides it.

The inner loop runs from start to finish on every single pass of the outer loop. The outer loop makes {{r}} passes (i from 0, with <), and each time the inner loop makes {{c}} passes (j from 1, with <=), so count++ runs {{r}} times {{c}} = {{expected}} times. Adding the two numbers instead of multiplying is the usual mistake.

question: NPC: A table for a loop inside a loop
intro: Nia rules three columns on the wall: i, the values j takes, and what gets printed. “A nested loop looks frightening until you give it a table. One row of the table for each pass of the outer loop.”

beats.say: Here is a loop inside a loop. The inner loop’s limit is i, so it changes from row to row.
Rule one: for each single pass of the outer loop, the inner loop runs all the way from its start to its end.

steps.say:
Row one of my table: i is 0. The inner loop starts j at 0, and 0 <= 0 is true, so one # is printed. Then j becomes 1, and 1 <= 0 is false, so the inner loop is over.
println() with nothing in the brackets just ends the line. Table so far: i = 0, j took the value 0, printed #.

beats.say: Row one of my table: i is 0. The inner loop starts j at 0, and 0 <= 0 is true, so one # is printed. Then j becomes 1, and 1 <= 0 is false, so the inner loop is over.
println() with nothing in the brackets just ends the line. Table so far: i = 0, j took the value 0, printed #.

check.prompt: Now i is 1. How many times does the inner loop run?
check.why: j starts again from 0 and keeps going while j <= 1, so it takes the values 0 and 1.

steps.say:
So the second line is ##, and then i becomes 2, 2 < 2 is false, and everything stops. Output: # on one line, ## on the next.
The pattern to keep: the outer loop decides WHICH row you are on, the inner loop decides WHAT goes in that row. And j starts over on every row.

beats.say: So the second line is ##, and then i becomes 2, 2 < 2 is false, and everything stops. Output: # on one line, ## on the next.
The pattern to keep: the outer loop decides WHICH row you are on, the inner loop decides WHAT goes in that row. And j starts over on every row.

outro: “The next monster’s inner loop starts at i instead of stopping at i. Same table, different numbers. Fill it in row by row.”

question: Here the inner loop starts at i. Trace it row by row: what does it print?
feedback: When i is 0, j takes 0, 1, 2 and three stars are printed; when i is 1, j takes 1, 2 (two stars); when i is 2, j takes only 2 (one star). println() with no argument ends each row. Because the inner loop starts at i rather than 0, each row is one star shorter than the last.

correct: It compiles, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the second line runs
incorrect: It does not compile: the compiler can see that index 3 is out of range
It compiles and runs: the array grows to make room for a fourth element
It compiles and runs: a write outside the array is silently ignored
feedback: new int[3] makes exactly three slots, numbered 0, 1 and 2, so index 3 does not exist. The compiler does not check index values, even literal ones, so the mistake surfaces only at run time, as an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: "Index 3 out of bounds for length 3". A Java array never grows (that is what ArrayList is for), and Java never quietly ignores a bad index.

question:
Complete the loop header so that it works for an int[] named scores of any size:

for (int i = 0; i < scores.___; i++)
feedback: Every array carries its size in a field called length, written with no parentheses: scores.length. A String, in contrast, has a method, text.length(), with parentheses, and the lists you will meet later use size(). Writing scores.length() or scores.size() for an array does not compile.

question:
int[] a = {5, 8, 15, 16};

Match each expression to its value.
feedback: Indices start at 0, so a[0] is the first element, 5. a.length is the number of elements, 4, which makes a[a.length - 1] the last element, a[3] = 16. a[1] + a[2] adds two elements: 8 + 15 = 23. An index can be any int expression: a[0] - 3 is 2, so a[a[0] - 3] is a[2] = 15.

question:
int[] nums = new int[{{n}}];

Which index does the expression  nums[nums.length - {{k}}]  refer to? (Give the index, not the value stored there.)
feedback_template: nums.length is {{n}}, so the index is {{n}} - {{k}} = {{expected}}. Since the last valid index is always length - 1, counting back from length is the standard way to reach elements at the end of an array. nums[nums.length] itself is one past the end and throws an exception.

question: Which of these lines compile and create an array of three ints?
feedback: Braces list the starting values; new int[3] makes three slots that each start at 0; new int[]{...} combines the two. Parentheses and square brackets are not array syntax in Java (square-bracket lists are Python and JavaScript). The size never goes on the left: the type is just int[], and the length belongs to the array object that new or the braces create.

question: Arrange these lines into a program that adds up the array and prints 27.
feedback: The array has to exist before sum can be started from nums[0]; the loop then adds the remaining elements, from index 1 up to the last valid index (i < nums.length); and the total is printed only after the closing brace, once the loop has finished. Printing inside the loop would show a running total three times over.

question: This is a for-each loop: read the header as "for each int s in scores". What is printed?
feedback: On each pass the for-each loop (also called the enhanced for) copies the next element into s: first 3, then 5, then 8. There is no index, no length and no condition to get wrong, so an off-by-one error is impossible. When you need every element and do not need its position, this is the form to prefer. total ends as 3 + 5 + 8 = 16.

question: Write the for-each loop header, ending with its opening brace, that visits every element of the int[] named scores, calling the current element s.
feedback: The shape is for (elementType name : array). The type comes first, as in any declaration, then the name for the current element, a colon (read it as "in"), and the array. var also works, because Java can infer int from the array. There is no counter, no condition and no update.

question: int[] a holds four values. Each loop below uses a[i] in its body (or x, for the for-each). Which headers visit every element exactly once without throwing an exception?
feedback: Valid indices run from 0 to a.length - 1. Starting at 0 with i < a.length covers exactly those, and the for-each covers them with no index at all. Using <= reaches a[4], which throws. Starting at 1 misses the first element, and stopping at a.length - 1 with < misses the last. The backwards loop starts at a[4], which throws at once; a correct one runs from a.length - 1 down to i >= 0.

question: NPC: Same scroll, or same words?
intro: Nia lays two scrolls side by side. Both say dragon. “You can ask two different questions about these. Java has a different tool for each, and mixing them up is the most famous bug in the language.”

steps.say:
Question one: is this the very same scroll? Question two: do the two scrolls say the same words?
A String variable does not hold the text itself. It holds a reference: an arrow pointing at a String object somewhere in memory.
On Strings, == compares the references: do both arrows point at the same object? The method .equals() compares the content: are the characters the same?

beats.say: Question one: is this the very same scroll? Question two: do the two scrolls say the same words?
A String variable does not hold the text itself. It holds a reference: an arrow pointing at a String object somewhere in memory.
On Strings, == compares the references: do both arrows point at the same object? The method .equals() compares the content: are the characters the same?
Watch both questions being asked about one String:
word was glued together while the program was running, so it is a brand-new String object. Its content is dragon, but it is not the same object as the literal "dragon".

check.prompt: What do the two println lines show?
check.why: Different objects, so == is false. Same characters, so .equals() is true.

steps.say:
Here is why this bug hides so well. Two identical literals written in your code ARE the same object. Java guarantees it. So == seems to work in every small test you write.
Then the text arrives from a Scanner, or is built at run time, and == quietly says false. To compare what two Strings say, use .equals().

beats.say: Here is why this bug hides so well. Two identical literals written in your code ARE the same object. Java guarantees it. So == seems to work in every small test you write.
Then the text arrives from a Scanner, or is built at run time, and == quietly says false. To compare what two Strings say, use .equals().

outro: “The next monster makes a second String object on purpose, with new. Ask both questions of it.”

question: new String("hi") makes a second String object with the same characters. What are the two lines of output?
feedback: a and b refer to two different String objects, so == (same object?) is false. Both contain the characters h and i, so .equals() (same content?) is true. You would not normally write new String(...) at all; it is here only to make a second object on purpose. Text typed by a user behaves the same way as b does.

question: Which of these statements about comparing Strings in Java are correct?
correct: == asks whether two String variables refer to the same object
.equals() asks whether two Strings contain the same characters
Text read with a Scanner can fail == against a literal with the same characters
Two identical literals in the source code are the same object, so == is true for them
incorrect: == compares the characters, as long as both Strings have the same length
.equals() gives false for two separate objects, even if their characters match
feedback: == on any object type, String included, compares references; .equals() compares content. Identical literals are guaranteed by the language to be one shared object, which is exactly why == appears to work in small tests. Strings that arrive at run time, from a Scanner, from concatenation or from new, are separate objects, and == on them is false even when the text matches. Length has nothing to do with it.

question: name is a String variable. Write the boolean expression (no if, no semicolon) that is true exactly when name contains the same characters as the literal "Nia".
feedback: Content is compared with the equals method: name.equals("Nia"). Writing it the other way round, "Nia".equals(name), is also correct. name == "Nia" compiles, but it asks whether the two are the same object, which fails as soon as name comes from user input.

question: The loop body doubles s. What does the last line print?
feedback: In a for-each loop, s is a copy of the current element, not the element itself. Doubling s changes the copy, which is thrown away at the end of the pass, so the array still holds 3, 5, 8. To change what is stored in an array you need the index: for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) { scores[i] = scores[i] * 2; }

question: A while loop with an if-else inside it, and integer division. What single number is printed?
feedback: Even values are halved and odd values become 3n + 1, so n goes 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is eight changes, and steps counts one per pass, so 8 is printed. The loop ends when n reaches 1 because 1 > 1 is false. Nobody can tell in advance how many passes this takes, which is why it is a while loop and not a counted for loop.

question: for-each, continue and break together. What is printed?
feedback: 12 is counted. 0 triggers continue, which skips the rest of that pass. 7 is counted. The next 0 is skipped as well. 30 triggers break, which ends the whole loop, so the final 5 is never looked at, even though it would have counted. alive is 2. Order matters too: the continue test comes first, so a zero can never reach the break test.
